questions.prompt: Why can a recursive function with depth 100,000 fail in Python even though it is correct?
options: Python forbids recursion deeper than 100
Every call adds a stack frame, the default limit is about 1000 frames, and Python does not optimize tail calls
Recursive functions always run in O(n²) time
The garbage collector frees frames too slowly
questions.explanation: Frames use memory (O(depth) space) and CPython guards against stack overflow with a recursion limit. Fixes: rewrite as a loop with an explicit stack, or restructure the algorithm. Raising the limit very high can crash the interpreter instead.

questions.prompt: How does functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128) differ from functools.cache?
options: lru_cache keeps at most 128 results and evicts the least recently used; cache is unbounded; both need hashable arguments

questions.explanation: Both memoize by the call arguments. `cache` is just `lru_cache(maxsize=None)`: it never evicts, so memory grows with the number of distinct calls. A bounded cache trades some recomputation for O(maxsize) memory.

questions.prompt: A depth-first traversal of a path graph with 100,000 nodes hits RecursionError. Which fix works reliably?
options: Raise sys.setrecursionlimit to 10**9
Add @cache to the recursive function
Rewrite it iteratively with an explicit stack (a list) of nodes still to visit
Catch RecursionError and retry
questions.explanation: An explicit stack lives on the heap, so its size is limited by memory rather than by the interpreter's frame limit: O(n) space, same O(n) time. A huge recursion limit can overflow the C stack and crash Python, @cache does nothing for depth, and retrying fails the same way.
